title: Faces of the sangha
hook: wise, powerful, forgetful, proud, gentle: all were welcome

segments.voice: Yesterday, even Devadatta, named in the Lotus Sutra as the Buddha's past teacher and promised buddhahood. Your line was even him. Today, the whole crowd in the robe.

Line them up the way the texts remember them. A man the texts call foremost in wisdom. His friend, foremost in powers. A slow monk who couldn't keep a single verse in his head. A former charioteer too proud to take advice from anyone. A cousin so gentle he served as attendant, bringing water and keeping the door. Different speeds, different tempers, different flaws, all in one robe color. None of them was turned away for being who he was.

First, the word. Sangha means community, an assembly. In the narrow sense it's the order of monks and nuns; in a wider sense, some Buddhists use it for everyone who walks the path together. It's the third of the Three Jewels, beside the Buddha and the dhamma, the things a Buddhist goes to for refuge. Second, the wise and the powerful. Sariputta and Moggallana, the two chief disciples, are the faces people expect: the texts praise one for wisdom and the other for power. Third, the slow and the proud. In a commentary story, Culapanthaka's own brother told him to leave the order, because he couldn't learn one verse. The Buddha handed him a clean white cloth instead, and as he rubbed it gray, he understood. And Channa, the former charioteer, was so stubborn that the Buddha, before he died, said the monks should give him the higher penalty: no one would speak to him or advise him. The Vinaya says that silence brought him to his senses, and he too awakened. Fourth, one path, different paces. Ananda, gentle and loyal, was still not awakened when the Buddha died. The sangha was never a gallery of finished people. It was a room where people at very different points sat side by side. And the welcome had a shape. It wasn't approval of every flaw. Channa's pride was met with a hard silence, but the silence was meant to bring him back, not to push him out.
screen: `SANGHA: THE COMMUNITY.` · `WISE AND POWERFUL, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `SLOW AND PROUD, STILL WELCOME.` · `ONE PATH, DIFFERENT PACES.` · then, large: `ALL WERE WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Bring one friend to mind, and let one of their flaws come up, the habit that wears on you: running late, talking over people, forgetting what you told them. Don't fix it, and don't excuse it; just set it beside everything else they are, the way the sangha set the slow monk beside the wise one. The flaw is real, and the friend is more than the flaw.
Sangha. The community: wise, powerful, forgetful, proud and gentle, all welcomed and practicing side by side. Today's word.
Your line: all were welcome. Wise or slow, proud or gentle, there was room. That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhists go for refuge to the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, often reciting the three refuges in Pali at the start of a gathering, and teachers retell the disciples' stories to show that people of every temperament walked the path.

chat.says: Did you have to be wise or disciplined already to join the Buddha's sangha?
options: No. Slow, proud and gentle people were all welcomed, at different paces.
Yes. Only people who were already awakened were let in.
No, and once you were inside, nobody ever addressed your flaws.
chat.meaning: The sangha held Culapanthaka, Channa and Ananda beside the wise. The welcome had a shape: Channa's pride met a silence meant to bring him back.

Three Jewels.meaning: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha: a Buddhist's refuge

Moggallana.meaning: a chief disciple, praised for power

Culapanthaka.meaning: the slow monk who understood while rubbing a white cloth

Channa.meaning: the proud former charioteer, brought back by silence

notes: This is a looking-back day: Sariputta (728, 730), Moggallana (729), Culapanthaka (772), Channa (752) and Ananda (732–738) were taught earlier; check that the summaries match those days' scripts.

Channa: DN 16 has the Buddha prescribe the brahmadanda; Cullavagga 11 tells how Ananda delivers it and Channa, distressed, later becomes an arahant. 'That silence brought him to his senses' is a paraphrase; confirm.
Culapanthaka: 'his own brother told him to leave' follows the Dhammapada commentary (Mahapanthaka); confirm.
howItsDone: 'often reciting the three refuges in Pali at the start of a gathering' describes common Theravada practice; confirm phrasing for a pan-Buddhist path.
